[[People's Army of Vietnam|PAVN]] claim: 100,000+ casualties (including ~40,000 killed/missing){{cite web|url=http://www.historynet.com/north-vietnamese-armys-1972-eastertide-offensive.htm |title= North Vietnamese Army's 1972 Eastertide Offensive|author=web site|year=1997|publisher=web site|access-date=1 February 2010}}{{Citation |last=Sorley|first=Lewis|year=1999|title=Courage and Blood: South Vietnam's Repulse of the 1972 Easter Invasion|publisher=[[United States Army War College]]|publication-place= |page= |url=https://press.armywarcollege.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1933&context=parameters|access-date=|ref=none}} | yearcost1 = }} {{Campaignbox Vietnam War}} '''1972 in the Vietnam War''' saw foreign involvement in [[South Vietnam]] slowly declining. Three allies, [[Australia]], [[New Zealand]] and [[Thailand]], which had each contributed military contingents, left South Vietnam this year. The [[United States]] continued to participate in combat, primarily with air power to assist the South Vietnamese, while negotiators in Paris tried to hammer out a peace agreement and withdrawal strategy for the United States. On 30 March [[North Vietnam]] launched the Nguyễn Huệ or [[Easter Offensive]], a massive conventional invasion of South Vietnam. This led to a large increase in U.S. airpower and airstrikes to defend South Vietnam and a resumption of bombing of North Vietnam. By September the South Vietnamese had regained most of the territory lost in the offensive and the North Vietnamese returned to negotiations. [[Operation Linebacker II]] in mid to late December saw intensive bombing around [[Hanoi]] and [[Haiphong]]. ==January== ; 1 January U.S. military personnel in South Vietnam numbered 156,800 while [[Free World Military Assistance Forces]] (largely [[Republic of Korea Army]]) numbered 53,900.{{cite book|last=Willbanks|first=James|title=Vietnam War Almanac: An In-Depth Guide to the Most Controversial Conflict in American History|publisher=Simon and Schuster|year=2013|isbn=9781626365285}}{{rp|387}} The South Vietnamese government announced that there had been 20 breaches of the New Year's ceasefire resulting in nine South Vietnamese and 16 [[People's Army of Vietnam]] (PAVN)/[[Vietcong]] VC killed.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon charges truce violations|date=1 January 1972|page=1}} U.S. aircraft flew more than 200 sorties to attack PAVN supply lines in [[Cambodia]] and [[Laos]].{{rp|387}} The U.S. Army reported that between 1969 and 1971 over 700 [[Fragging]]s occurred resulting in 82 dead and 631 wounded.{{rp|387}} ;2 January [[President of the United States|President]] [[Richard Nixon]] announced that unilateral U.S. troop withdrawals from South Vietnam would continue, but a residual force of 25–35,000 would remain until all U.S. [[U.S. prisoners of war during the Vietnam War|prisoners of war]] (POWs) were released.{{rp|387}} South Vietnam withdrew more than 10,000 soldiers from operations in Cambodia to bolster defenses around [[Saigon]] in preparation for an expected PAVN/VC during [[Tết]].{{rp|388}} ;3 January [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[United States Senate|Senator]] [[George McGovern]] accused Nixon of deceiving the public by suggesting that the North Vietnamese had rejected a release of POWs in return for a firm date for withdrawal of U.S. forces, saying that Nixon was using the issue to justify bombing the North and propping up the government of [[Leaders of South Vietnam|President of South Vietnam]] [[Nguyễn Văn Thiệu]].{{rp|388}} [[Max Frankel]] writing in ''[[The New York Times]]'' stated that Nixon was buying time to build up South Vietnam through [[Vietnamization]] and improve the position of anti-communist forces in Cambodia and Laos.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Buying time in the Vietnam War|author=Max Frankel|date=4 January 1972|page=3}} PAVN ambushed a U.S. infantry patrol {{convert|40|mi}} northeast of Saigon and then shot down three [[Medevac]] helicopters, resulting in one U.S. killed.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. patrol ambushed|date=4 January 1972|page=5}} ;4 January A [[Royal Lao Army]] (RLA) spokesman said that a PAVN force, supported by two [[Vietnam People's Air Force]] (VPAF) [[MiG]] jets, had destroyed a bridge on Route 13, {{convert|20|mi}} from the besieged RLA base at [[Long Tieng]]. Seven RLA and 14 PAVN were killed in the attack.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Enemy troops, aided by MIG's destroy a key bridge in Laos|date=5 January 1972|page=6}} ;5 January A [[United States Air Force]] (USAF) [[Republic F-105 Thunderchief|F-105G]] escorting [[Boeing B-52 Stratofortress|B-52 Stratofortresses]] on a bombing mission over Laos attacked a PAVN radar-guided antiaircraft gun {{convert|10|mi}} north of the [[Ban Karai Pass]] in the first "protective reaction" strike of the year. B-52s also bombed PAVN positions near [[Khe Sanh]].{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Gun site in North attacked by jet|author=Iver Peterson|date=6 January 1972|page=1}} The South Vietnamese [[Joint General Staff]] (JGS) announced that they were withdrawing from fixed bases in Cambodia and would in future rely on a 15,000 man airmobile and armored cavalry task force assigned to Military Region 3 to undertake operations there.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Change in strategy reported|date=6 January 1972|page=8}} North Vietnam announced that in order for the U.S. to secure the release of its POWs it must "completely end the war of aggression in Vietnam and remove all its troops from Vietnam" and "completely end the Vietnamization policy of continuing the war" which it denounced as a "plot to withdraw United States forces but still continue the war of American aggression by puppet forces under United States direction and with United States support and supplies."{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Hanoi ties P.O.W. issue to end of Vietnamization|date=6 January 1972|page=8}} ;6 January At the [[Paris Peace Talks]] the North Vietnamese reiterated their position that U.S. POWs would only be released once the U.S. withdrew all its forces and the U.S. "give up aggression, stop the "Vietnamization" of the war, pull out from South Vietnam all the troops... stop backing the Nguyễn Văn Thiệu bellicose puppet group."{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Enemy sets P.O.W. price: abandon Thieu and leave|author=Henry Giniger|date=7 January 1972|page=1}} Democratic Senator [[Edmund Muskie]] called for the U.S. to withdraw from South Vietnam regardless of the consequences saying that 55,000 American lives and $130 billion spent on the war had been "wasted."{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Muskie bid U.S. get out of war|author=James Naughten|date=7 January 1972|page=1}} ;8 January In response to [[India]]'s decision to upgrade its diplomatic relations with North Vietnam to ambassadorial level, South Vietnam announced that India could no longer be regarded as an impartial member of the [[International Control Commission]] and barred the new Indian chair of the commission from entering South Vietnam.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon bars Indian on control team|date=9 January 1972|page=20}} ;9 January A VC threw a grenade into a youth rally in [[Quy Nhon]] in an attempt to kill the [[Bình Định province]] chief, the grenade killed two teachers and seven students and wounded 110 others.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Grenade kills 9 and wounds 110 at youth rally in South Vietnam|date=9 January 1972|page=15}} RLA forces held off PAVN attacks on Ban Nhik, the last government position on the Boloven Plateau, {{convert|20|mi}} east of [[Pakse]]. In three days of fighting the RLA claimed to have killed more than 75 PAVN around Ban Nhik with a further 200 killed in airstrikes and reports of more than 200 wounded being taken to [[Paksong]].{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Laos troops hold off foe near key village in South|author=Tillman Durdin|date=10 January 1972|page=1}} ; 10 January The Cambodian [[Khmer National Army]] (ANK) withdrew from the town of [[Ponhea Kraek]] (Krek) near the [[Fishhook (Cambodia)|Fishhook]] abandoning the last remaining road link between Cambodia and South Vietnam. Further south in the [[Parrot's Beak, Cambodia|Parrot's Beak]] the South Vietnamese [[Army of the Republic of Vietnam]] (ARVN) began [[Operation Prek Ta]] against the PAVN in that area of Cambodia. The objective of the offensive was to disrupt the preparations of the North Vietnamese for an anticipated offensive on Tết, 15 February.Deac, Wilfed P. (1996), "Losing Ground to the Khmer Rouge", ''Vietnam Magazine,'' Dec 1996, http://www.historynet.com/losing-ground-to-the-khmer-rouge.htm {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110612213034/http://www.historynet.com/losing-ground-to-the-khmer-rouge.htm |date=2011-06-12 }}, accessed 9 Jun 2015 Former [[Vice President of the United States|Vice President]] [[Hubert Humphrey]] announced his candidacy for the Democratic presidential nomination and criticized the slow pace of withdrawal from South Vietnam, saying that if he had been elected in 1968 all U.S. forces would have been withdrawn already.{{rp|388}} ''The New York Times'' reported on the growing expectation of a PAVN offensive in the Central Highlands timed to coincide with Nixon's visit to China.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Fears of Tet drive are rising in Saigon|author=Craig R. Whitney|date=11 January 1972|page=3}} Three [[Communist Party of Thailand]] sappers attempted to destroy B-52s at [[U-Tapao Royal Thai Navy Airfield]], Thailand using grenades and satchel charges. One attacker was apparently killed in the attack, while the other two managed to cause minor damage to three B-52s before fleeing the base.{{cite book|last=Vick|first=Alan|title=Snakes in the Eagle's Nest: A history of ground attacks on air bases|publisher=RAND Corporation|year=1995|url=https://www.rand.org/content/dam/rand/pubs/monograph_reports/2006/MR553.pdf|isbn=9780833016294|pages=83–4|archive-date=2023-05-05|access-date=2022-01-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230505085556/https://www.rand.org/content/dam/rand/pubs/monograph_reports/2006/MR553.pdf|url-status=live}} ;11 January The South Vietnamese military acknowledged that it was withdrawing its forces from Krek and other locations in Cambodia in preparation for an expected PAVN offensive during Tết.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon pulls back forces in Krek area of Cambodia|date=12 January 1972|page=2}} The PAVN fired two [[S-75 Dvina|SA-2]] [[Surface-to-air missile]]s (SAMs) at a USAF [[McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom II|F-4 Phantom]] near [[Tchepone]], showing the continuous improvement of PAVN air defences in Laos. A USAF F-4 fired two missiles at a radar site in North Vietnam in a "protective reaction" strike while escorting B-52s in a bombing raid on the Ban Karai Pass.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. jet is target of missiles from deepest site yet in Laos|author=Craig R. Whitney|date=12 January 1972|page=2}} RLA forces abandoned Ban Nhik after four days of heavy fighting.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Laotians report losses|date=12 January 1972|page=2}} ;12 January [[Le Duc Tho]], [[Politburo]] member and secret negotiator for North Vietnam in the Paris Peace Talks, cabled the head of [[Central Office for South Vietnam]] (COSVN) in South Vietnam that "we and the enemy are preparing for a ferocious confrontation... during the upcoming spring and summer." In addition to supporting the PAVN troops in South Vietnam, Tho instructed COSVN to devote attention to attacking the [[Civil Operations and Revolutionary Development Support]] (CORDS) pacification program] and to the political struggle in the cities of South Vietnam.''(FRUS) Foreign Relations of the United States, 1969-1976, Volume VIII, Vietnam, January–October 1972'', Document 1, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1969-76v08/d1#fn3 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150618161702/https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1969-76v08/d1#fn3 |date=2015-06-18 }}, accessed 8 Jun 2015 The 2,400-man ANK 22nd Brigade deployed near Krek dissolved itself with officers and soldiers shedding their uniforms and fleeing into South Vietnam.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Entire 2,400-Man Cambodian Brigade flees posts and deserts|date=13 January 1972|page=12}} More than 34 PAVN/VC shelling and ground attacks were reported in the most intensive attacks in three months. A VC unit attacked a 30-man ARVN patrol in the [[Mekong Delta]] killing three, with eleven missing. The PAVN/VC shot down a U.S. [[Bell UH-1 Iroquois|UH-1]] helicopter in the Mekong Delta killing all four crewmen.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Enemy attacks reach a 3-month record|date=13 January 1972|page=16}} Cambodian and South Vietnamese forces began a joint operation near Ang Tassom {{convert|42|mi}} south of [[Phnom Penh]].{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon troops in new Cambodian action|date=14 January 1972|page=3}} ;13 January Nixon announced that 70,000 American troops would be pulled out of South Vietnam by 1 May, cutting the existing force of 139,000 by half.{{rp|389}} PAVN/VC attacks continued throughout South Vietnam conducting 26 attacks resulting in 33 PAVN/VC killed and 15 ARVN killed. Two USAF F-105Gs fired missiles at a SAM site on the Laos-North Vietnam border, while escorting B-52s.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon's forces hit hard|date=14 January 1972|page=3}} ;14 January A USAF F-105G destroyed a SAM site {{convert|3|mi}} north of the [[Vietnamese Demilitarized Zone]] (DMZ) while escorting [[United States Navy]] fighter-bombers attacking the [[Ho Chi Minh Trail]].{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. jet apparently destroys missile unit just north of DMZ|date=15 January 1972|page=12}} ;15 January [[Military Assistance Command, Vietnam]] (MACV) reported that the North Vietnamese were moving more SAMs closer to the DMZ with an F-105G destroying a SAM site in the eastern DMZ and two SA-2s being fired on an F-105 flying {{convert|15|mi}} north of the DMZ near the Laos-North Vietnam border. In ongoing attacks throughout South Vietnam 89 PAVN/VC, 15 ARVN and 15 civilians were reported killed.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Enemy advances SAM launchers closer to the border|date=16 January 1972|page=1}} RLA forces were flown into Long Tieng and were reported to have broken the siege of the base, recapturing Skyline Ridge {{convert|2|mi}} north of the base.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Siege reported broken|date=16 January 1972|page=2}} ;16 January Leaders of 46 Protestant, Catholic, and Jewish organizations met in Kansas City and asked for the withdrawal of American military personnel from South Vietnam and a cut-off in aid to the South Vietnamese government.{{cite book|last=Summers|first=Harry|title=the Vietnam War Almanac|publisher=Presidio Press|year=1999|isbn=978-0891416920}}{{rp|55}} USAF jets engaged a VPAF [[Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21|MiG-21]] jet over northern Laos for the first time in a year. A PAVN/VC mortar attack on [[Cam Ranh Base]] killed seven ARVN.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. says its jets encountered MiG over north Laos|date=17 January 1972|page=1}} ;17 January In a secret letter to Thiệu, Nixon warned that his refusal to sign a peace agreement to end the war would make it impossible for the U.S. to continue support for South Vietnam.{{rp|389}} U.S. aircraft flew more than 200 airstrikes against PAVN supply lines in Laos to disrupt preparations for a PAVN offensive and returned fire against PAVN SAM sites near the Ban Karai Pass.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Foe's supply trail in Laos pounded by U.S. aircraft|date=18 January 1972|page=3}} ;18 January [[Seymour Hersh]] who wrote the first detailed account of the [[My Lai massacre]] reported that a U.S. Army investigation showed that more than 347 civilians had been killed at My Lai, rather than less than 200 as previously reported and that more than 90 civilians had been killed in the nearby village of My Khe 4 on the same day.{{rp|389}} Two VPAF MiGs conducted an unsuccessful hit and run attack on USAF F-4s over northern Laos, firing three air-to-air missiles before fleeing back across the border. USAF aircraft conducted more than 250 airstrikes over Laos.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. reports MiG attack on jets over Laos failed|date=19 January 1972|page=6}} ;19 January A U.S. Navy F-4B piloted by Lieutenant [[Duke Cunningham]] and Lieutenant j.g. [[William P. Driscoll]] engaged and shot down a VPAF MiG-21 near [[Quang Lang Air Base]] scoring the first U.S. aerial victory in 22 months.{{cite book|last=Sherwood|first=John|title=Nixon's Trident: Naval Power in Southeast Asia, 1968-1972|publisher=Government Printing Office|year=2015|url=https://www.history.navy.mil/research/publications/publications-by-subject/nixons-trident.html|isbn=9780160928697|page=54|archive-date=2022-01-25|access-date=2022-01-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220125104742/https://www.history.navy.mil/research/publications/publications-by-subject/nixons-trident.html|url-status=live}}{{PD-notice}} Reporters were flown into Long Tieng for the first time ever to view operations at the previously secret base.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=CIA aided Laos base hit hard|author=Craig R. Whitney|date=20 January 1972|page=1}} A U.S. UH-1 helicopter was shot down {{convert|1|mi}} southwest of Khe Sanh while attempting to rescue the crew of a shot-down F-4. Two crewmembers were killed and a further six injured.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Destruction of 2 enemy gun sites in DMZ by U.S. F-4's reported|date=24 January 1972|page=4}} ; 20 January The head of MACV, General [[Creighton Abrams]] cabled Washington that "the enemy [North Vietnam] is preparing and positioning his forces for a major offensive.... There is no doubt this is to be a major campaign." Abrams requested additional authority to use U.S. American air power to mount an effective defense. More than 10,000 ARVN began a sweep of PAVN/VC base areas in a plantation {{convert|45|mi}} northwest of Saigon as part of ongoing efforts to disrupt an anticipated Tết offensive.{{rp|389}} More than 12,000 [[Royal Thai Army]] and other paramilitary forces began an offensive against an estimated 150-200 communists in the mountainous [[Lom Sak District]] of northeast Thailand.{{rp|389}} ;22 January Heavy fighting continued on Skyline Ridge in Laos and the RLA abandoned Phou Khoun northwest of Long Tieng, however Laotian Premier Souvanna Phouma said that further U.S. aid would not be required unless the situation deteriorated further.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Souvanna Phouma says more U.S. help isn't needed yet|author=Craig R. Whitney|date=23 January 1972|page=3}} The JGS reported that 35 PAVN/VC had been killed for the loss of four ARVN, mostly in fighting in Bình Định province, while South Korean forces reported killing 38 PAVN/VC.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=73 of foe reported slain|date=23 January 1972|page=3}} ;23 January U.S. jets attacked two antiaircraft gun sites in the DMZ and one east of the Ban Karai Pass. The JGS reported killing 38 PAVN/VC and capturing two for the loss of two ARVN. ;24 January U.S. jets carried out a further three "protective reaction" strikes against PAVN antiaircraft sites, two near the Ban Karai Pass and one near [[Đồng Hới]].{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. reports 3 more attacks in North|author=Fox Butterfield|date=25 January 1972|page=12}} [[United States Army Vietnam]] acknowledged that a regulation had been passed two weeks previously allowing "local national guests" onto U.S. bases, effectively sanctioning [[Prostitution in Vietnam|prostitution]] since local towns were declared off limits except to soldiers on official duties.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. now admitting prostitutes to some of its Vietnam bases|date=25 January 1972|page=12}} ; 25 January Nixon revealed that National Security Adviser [[Henry Kissinger]] had been meeting secretly with North Vietnamese representatives for more than 2 years. He also revealed the U.S. peace plan that had been proposed to Hanoi. Nixon proposed that, within six months of an agreement, all U.S. military be withdrawn from South Vietnam, POWs exchanged, an internationally supervised ceasefire implemented and a presidential election held in South Vietnam. Nixon did not demand the withdrawal of North Vietnamese military forces from South Vietnam."Address to the Nation on Plan for Peace in Vietnam", Miller Center. http://millercenter.org/president/nixon/speeches/speech-3879 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150317023055/http://millercenter.org/president/nixon/speeches/speech-3879 |date=2015-03-17 }}, accessed 8 Jun 2015 In a radio address, Thiệu endorsed the proposal, including the provision that he and the Vice President would resign one month before the presidential election.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Thieu, on radio, endorses election plan|author=Craig R. Whitney|date=26 January 1972|page=11}} ;25-6 January The [[Republic of Vietnam Air Force]] (RVNAF) reported sighting six PAVN [[T-54]] tanks {{convert|7|mi}} south of [[Ben Het Camp]]. RVNAF aircraft attacked PAVN convoys {{convert|9|mi}} west of Ben Het Camp and 7 miles southwest of Firebase 5 in the [[Central Highlands (Vietnam)|Central Highlands]].{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. attacks radar in the North for the 19th time this month|date=27 January 1972|page=16}} ;26 January North Vietnam rejected the U.S. peace proposal and submitted a counterproposal at the same time as publishing bellicose messages alluding to a coming offensive.{{rp|390}} A USAF F-4 carried out a "protective reaction" strike on a SAM site near Đồng Hới. The JGS reported that 31 PAVN/VC had been killed in operations in the Mekong Delta. ;27 January North Vietnam criticized the U.S. for making public the details of secret peace talks and repeated its demand for the immediate and unconditional withdrawal of U.S. military personnel from South Vietnam and the removal of the Thiệu government.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Foe again insists U.S. set pullout and expel Thieu|date=28 January 1972|page=1}} The Nixon administration acknowledged that an offer of up to $2.5 billion of U.S. aid had been offered to North Vietnam as part of a $7.5 billion reconstruction aid package for Indochina.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Aide said U.S. suggested $2.5 billion help to Hanoi|date=28 January 1972|page=1}} ;28 January The JGS reported that 116 PAVN/VC had been killed in two battles in the Central Highlands.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Two enemy attacks reported in Vietnam|date=28 January 1972|page=7}} MACV and the JGS released casualty figures for the war to date, reporting 45,639 U.S., 138,803 South Vietnamese and 792,437 PAVN/VC killed. In a performance at a [[White House]] gala dinner by the [[Ray Conniff]] Singers, one of the singers, Carole Feraci, held up a banner reading "Stop the Killing" and said "President Nixon, stop bombing human beings, animals and vegetation. You go to church on Sundays and pray to Jesus Christ, if Jesus Christ were here tonight, you would not dare to drop another bomb."{{cite news|title=Richard Nixon and the Oobie-Doobie Girl|author=Bob Thompson|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=27 July 1997|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/magazine/1997/07/27/richard-nixon-and-the-oobie-doobie-girl/3e23c6d9-eb6c-44a8-bae8-daae0ab6b205/}} ;29 January ''The New York Times'' reported on the widespread corruption throughout South Vietnam and also on the confusion within the South Vietnamese government in reporting on the war with frequent retractions and denials.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times |title=Bribes to evade draft or pass a test or get a job make corruption a way of life in South Vietnam |author=Gloria Emerson |author-link=Gloria Emerson |date=30 January 1972 |page=3}} ;30 January U.S. intelligence sources stated that PAVN political officers had instructed PAVN/VC soldiers that decisive blows would be made while Nixon visited China in February and U.S. Army Chief of Staff General [[William Westmoreland]] on a visit to Saigon said that an offensive was expected in February.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Hanoi said to mass force for offensive in February|author=Tad Szulc|date=31 January 1972|page=1}} ;31 January North Vietnam released a peace proposal it had made to the U.S. in June 1971 together with other correspondence relating to the secret talks conducted with Kissinger, in an apparent attempt to counter any propaganda gains the U.S. had made earlier in the month by revealing such talks.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Hanoi discloses peace proposals it made in Paris|author=Henry Giniger|date=1 February 1972|page=1}} The JGS reported that three PAVN tanks had been destroyed by RVNAF aircraft in the Central Highlands and that 54 PAVN and nine ARVN had been killed in fighting along the DMZ over the weekend with more than 200 rockets and mortar rounds hitting ARVN bases on 29 January.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Three tanks reported destroyed|date=31 January 1972|page=14}} The Cambodian government was reported to have approached the Soviet Embassy to initiate peace talks with North Vietnam that would provide for an internationally supervised withdrawal of PAVN forces to the east of the Mekong River and north of Route 7.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Cambodia Asks Talks Through Soviet|date=1 February 1972|page=13}} [[David Morrell (writer)|David Morrell]]'s novel ''[[First Blood (novel)|First Blood]]'' about a troubled homeless Vietnam veteran named Rambo is published. R. The battle was the first phase of the [[Easter Offensive in southern Cambodia and the Mekong Delta]].{{cite book|last=Ngo|first=Quang Truong|title=The Easter Offensive of 1972|publisher=U.S. Army Center of Military History|year=1980|url=https://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a324505.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200813062844/https://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a324505.pdf|url-status=live|archive-date=August 13, 2020}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|143–5}} ;23 March The United States boycotted peace negotiations in Paris with the North Vietnamese, citing the failure of North Vietnam to negotiate seriously.{{rp|395}} North Vietnamese sources described the POW issue as a smokescreen being used by Nixon to divert from peace talks and prolong the war.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=P.O.W.'s secondary, Hanoi says|author=Seymour Hersh|date=24 March 1972|page=1}} ;23 March - 24 October The ''Lavelle Affair'' began when USAF General [[John D. Correll|magazine=Air Force Magazine|date=1 November 2006|url=https://www.airforcemag.com/article/1106lavelle/|archive-date=19 July 2020|access-date=19 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200719070736/https://www.airforcemag.com/article/1106lavelle/|url-status=live}} ;24 March PAVN/Khmer Rouge sappers blew up the [[Chroy Changva Bridge|Japanese Bridge]] in Phnom Penh, collapsing several spans of the only highway bridge across the [[Tonlé Sap River]] and killing three civilians. ARVN forces engaged PAVN troops {{convert|18|mi}} southwest of Huế, killing 53 PAVN.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Booby trap kills 2 G.I.'s|date=30 March 1972|page=11}} ;30 March [[File:DRVA.jpg|thumb|right|PAVN M46 130mm guns]] The long anticipated offensive by the PAVN/VC began. Called the '''Nguyễn Huệ Offensive''' or '''Chiến dịch Xuân hè 1972''' in Vietnamese and the [[Easter Offensive]] in English, three PAVN divisions (30,000–40,000 men) with support from tanks and artillery crossed the DMZ or came from Laos to the west to attack the ARVN 3rd Division in the [[First Battle of Quảng Trị]]. Although a PAVN offensive had been expected, the invasion across the DMZ was a surprise and the ARVN was ill-prepared. Several small firebases were overrun within hours. Storms and cloud cover hindered U.S. and RVNAF air support.{{rp|395–6}} North Vietnam's military objectives in launching what would be a three-pronged offensive were the capture of the cities of [[Quảng Trị ward|Quang Tri]] in the northern part of South Vietnam, Kontum in the Central Highlands and [[An Lộc, Bình Phước|An Loc]] in the south."The History Place--Vietnam War 1969-1972", http://www.historyplace.com/unitedstates/vietnam/index-1969.html {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211125175007/http://www.historyplace.com/unitedstates/vietnam/index-1969.html |date=2021-11-25 }}, accessed 16 Jun 2015 Other objectives were believed to be to impress the North Vietnamese people and the Communist world with its determination, reinvigorate antiwar sentiment in the U.S. and undermine Nixon's reelection chances, disrupt Vietnamization and undermine the Thiệu government and seize territory ahead of any peace settlement.{{rp|396}} A USAF AC-130E gunship operated by the 16th Special Operations Squadron was shot down by antiaircraft fire over Laos, but all 15 crewmen survived and were rescued. ;31 March [[VAL-4]], the U.S. Navy's last combat unit in South Vietnam conducted its last mission and was disestablished on 10 April 1972.{{rp|396}} ==April== ;1-27 April [[Operation Fa Ngum]] was an RLA operation to capture the villages of Ban Ngik and Laongam as bases for incursions onto the Ho Chi Minh Trail. The RLA captured Laongam, but were repulsed by the PAVN in their attacks on Ban Ngik.{{rp|340–1}} ; 2 April The ARVN 56th Regiment, 3rd Division numbering about 1,500 soldiers at [[Camp Carroll]] surrendered to the PAVN. Camp Carroll was important to South Vietnam because of its [[M107 self-propelled gun|M107]] 175 mm artillery with a range of up to {{convert|20|mi|km}}. The capture of Camp Carroll gave the PAVN control of western [[Quảng Trị Province]].{{rp|24–30}} With the city of [[Đông Hà]] near the DMZ threatened, Nixon authorized U.S. naval vessels offshore to strike at the PAVN with warplanes and naval gunfire. Captain [[John Ripley (USMC)|John Ripley]] an adviser to the Vietnamese Marines spent three hours under the road bridge at Đông Hà installing demolition charges to destroy the bridge.{{cite book|last=Melson|first=Charles|title=U.S. Marines In Vietnam: The War That Would Not End, 1971–1973|publisher=History and Museums Division, Headquarters, U.S. Marine Corps|year=1991|url=https://archive.org/details/TheWarThatWouldNotEnd|isbn=978-1482384055}}{{PD-notice}}{{rp|56–60}} ;2-14 April [[File:Iceal gene hambleton.jpg|thumb|right|Iceal Hambleton]] Lieutenant Colonel [[Iceal Hambleton]] was the sole survivor of an [[Douglas B-66 Destroyer|EB-66]] shot down near Đông Hà. His [[Rescue of Bat 21 Bravo|rescue]] was the longest and most costly search and rescue mission during the war resulting in the loss of five aircraft, 11 U.S. killed and two captured. The rescue diverted U.S. aircraft from supporting the ARVN in the defense of Quảng Trị Province.{{Cite book|last1=Stoffey|first1=Robert|last2=Holloway|first2=James|title=Fighting to Leave: The Final Years of America's War in Vietnam, 1972-1973|date=5 September 2008|publisher=Zenith Press|isbn=978-0-760333105|page=69}} ;3 April The U.S. accused North Vietnam of invading South Vietnam in "flagrant violation" of both the [[1954 Geneva Conference|1954 Geneva Accords]] and the November 1968 understanding that led to the end of [[Operation Rolling Thunder]], the U.S. bombing of North Vietnam and warned that all retaliatory options were open.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. says Hanoi 'invaded' South, keeps all reprisal options open; Air armada prepared to attack|author=Bernard Gwertzman|date=3 April 1972|page=1}} Newspapers in Saigon were instructed by the National Press Center that they should only publish the Government's official reports on the fighting in Quảng Trị Province and threatened to take action against [[United Press International|UPI]] for a "completely false" account of the surrender of Camp Carroll.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon restricts its press on war|author=Fox Butterfield|date=3 April 1972|page=9}} The RLA reported that it had recaptured three of the four positions on Skyline Ridge that had been lost earlier to the PAVN.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Laotians recapture 3 helicopter pads|date=3 April 1972|page=9}} ;4 April Nixon authorized increased bombing of PAVN troops in South Vietnam and B-52 strikes against North Vietnam. He said, "These bastards have never been bombed like they're going to be bombed this time." The PAVN attacked South Vietnamese positions in northern [[Binh Dinh province]] from their stronghold in the [[An Lão District, Bình Định|An Lao Valley]]. PAVN/VC forces overran many ARVN positions.{{cite book|last=Andrade|first=Dale|title=Trial by Fire: The 1972 Easter Offensive, America's Last Vietnam Battle|publisher=Hippocrene Books|year=1994|isbn=978-0781802864}}{{rp|252–9}} The {{USS|Kitty Hawk|CV-63|6}} joined two U.S. Navy aircraft carriers already operating off the coast of Vietnam.{{rp|396}} North Vietnam and the VC called for the resumption of the Paris Peace Talks, but this was rejected by the U.S. and South Vietnam with a South Vietnamese spokesman saying "It is ridiculous to talk about wanting to negotiate while carrying out an invasion."{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Enemy asks new Paris talks; Allies reply with indignant no|author=Henry Giniger|date=5 April 1972|page=17}} ;5 April In a televised address Thiệu stated that the decisive battle for the survival of South Vietnam was underway.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=New enemy offensive reported, drive towards Quangtri goes on; Thieu see battle for 'survival'|author=Joseph B. Treaster|date=6 April 1972|page=1}} U.S. jets destroyed the [[Bến Hải River]] Bridge in the DMZ.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Span linking Vietnams is destroyed, U.S. says|date=8 April 1972|page=11}} U.S. military sources criticized the defensive mentality of the South Vietnamese noting that ARVN units were retreating and relying on U.S. airpower rather than standing and fighting.{{rp|397}} ;5–7 April The second prong of the Easter Offensive was the movement across the border from Cambodia of the VC [[5th Infantry Division (Vietnam)|5th Division]] and an attack on 4,000 ARVN defenders at the [[Battle of Loc Ninh]]. [[Lộc Ninh, Bình Phước|Lộc Ninh]] was a small district town in [[Bình Long Province]], approximately {{convert|75|mi|km}} north of Saigon. Nearly all of the ARVN defenders were killed or surrendered.{{rp|398–420}} [[File:A-7s from USS Oriskany (CVA-34) dropping bombs over Vietnam c1972.jpg|thumb|right|U.S. Navy A-7s bomb North Vietnam]] ;6 April U.S. aircraft and warships began [[Operation Freedom Train]] (later renamed Operation Linebacker) a sustained program of attacks against North Vietnam. The initial targets were SAM sites and troop concentrations in and north of the DMZ.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. planes and warships attack missile sites in north near DMZ; Enemy troops press offensive|author=Craig R. Whitney|date=7 April 1972|page=1}} ;7 April Secretary of Defense [[Melvin Laird]] stated that the U.S. would continue bombing North Vietnam until it withdrew its forces that had invaded South Vietnam and showed interest in "serious" peace negotiations.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Laird says U.S. will bomb until North pulls back|author=William Beecher|date=8 April 1972|page=1}} North Vietnam appealed to the French government to use its influence with the U.S. to try to stop the bombing of North Vietnam.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Hanoi bid France to intercede with U.S.|date=8 April 1972|page=11}} ''The New York Times'' reported that the North Vietnamese invasion had stirred anger and patriotism among South Vietnamese.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Hanoi drive stirs patriotism in South|author=Fox Butterfield|date=8 April 1972|page=1}} ;8 April After capturing Lộc Ninh, PAVN/VC soldiers succeeded in surrounding the city of An Lộc, the capital of Bình Long Province and the objective of the southern prong of the Easter Offensive. Whitney|date=8 April 1972|page=1}} Abrams and Bunker advised the White House and the Pentagon that the PAVN offensive was likely to last for months and would only end when their objectives, believed to be the capture of Quảng Trị and [[Thừa Thiên Huế province|Thừa Thiên province]]s had been achieved or they were defeated.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Bunker, Abrams see a long drive|author=Craig R. Dee|year=1995|isbn=978-1566630795}}{{rp|265}} At dawn 2,000 PAVN launched an attack, led by tanks, against [[Firebase Pedro]] southwest of Quảng Trị. The PAVN tanks had outrun their infantry support and nine tanks were lost in a minefield around Pedro. An ARVN armored task force of eight [[M48 Patton|M48s]] and 12 [[M113 armored personnel carrier|M113s]] from the ARVN [[20th Tank Regiment (South Vietnam)|20th Tank Regiment]] were despatched from [[Quảng Trị Combat Base|Ái Tử Combat Base]] to support the Marines at Pedro. At the same time a flight of RVNAF [[Douglas A-1 Skyraider|A-1 Skyraiders]] arrived overhead and destroyed five tanks. When the ARVN armor arrived they destroyed five [[T-54/55|T-54s]] for no losses and captured one tank.{{rp|68–9}} The JGS ordered the [[21st Division (South Vietnam)|21st Division]] to move north to support the Battle of An Lộc as all of South Vietnam's reserve forces were already committed to containing the PAVN offensive.{{rp|398}} U.S. intelligence analysts said that all but one PAVN division had been committed to the offensive.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. analysts in Saigon say Hanoi threw all but one division into the offensive|author=Craig R. Whitney|date=10 April 1972|page=16}} Total PAVN losses during the attacks on Firebase Pedro, Đông Hà and [[Hải Lăng District]] were more than 1,000 killed and 30 tanks destroyed. A further 182 PAVN were killed in an attack on Firebase Bastogne/Phu Xuan for the loss of nine ARVN. [[I Corps (South Vietnam)|I Corps]] commander General [[Hoàng Xuân Lãm]] stated "This was the big battle. We have defeated them." and claimed that the PAVN advance had been stopped.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=North Vietnam's losses in a day in Quangtri area put at 1,000 men, 30 tanks|author=Fox Butterfield|date=11 April 1972|page=1}} The PAVN 12th Regiment, 3rd Division cut [[National Route 19 (Vietnam)|Route 19]] {{convert|8|mi}} east of An Khê.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Ankhe, now a Highlands ghost town, remains an important battlefield|author=Malcolm Browne|date=22 April 1972|page=10}} ; 10 April For the first time since 1967, U.S. B-52s bombed North Vietnam. Their priority targets were SAM sites described as "the most sophisticated air defenses in the history of air warfare.{{rp|305}} Nixon said that big powers had a special responsibility to discourage countries from attacking neighbouring countries, while the State Department said the offensive would not be possible without the Soviet Union supplying North Vietnam with sophisticated weapons.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Nixon indirectly criticizes Soviet arms aid to Hanoi|author=Bernard Gwertzman|date=11 April 1972|page=1}} The aircraft carrier {{USS|Midway|CV-41|6}} was ordered to Vietnam.{{rp|398}} ;11 April The PAVN lay siege to Firebase Bastogne/Phu Xuan losing 102 killed as an ARVN armored column tried for the third day to relieve the base. In fighting at Kampong Trach, Cambodia the ARVN killed 251 PAVN for the loss of seven ARVN killed.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon's forces said to repulse foe west of Hue|author=Fox Butterfield|date=12 April 1972|page=1}} North Vietnam stated that "every Vietnamese citizen has the right and duty to fight the American aggressor anywhere on Vietnamese territory." while continuing to claim that no North Vietnamese forces were fighting in South Vietnam.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Hanoi asserts right to battle the U.S. in North or South|date=12 April 1972|page=1}} North Vietnam again called for a resumption of the Paris Peace Talks and demanded that the U.S. stop bombing and other "acts of aggression."{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Hanoi aagains asks renewal of talks|date=12 April 1972|page=16}} Two more squadrons of B-52s were ordered to be deployed to Indochina, increasing the number to more than 130, the highest at any point of the war. In addition the [[United States Atlantic Fleet]] aircraft carrier {{USS|Saratoga|CV-60|6}} was ordered to deploy to Vietnam.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. cautiously optimistic but sends further B-52s|author=Terence Smith|date=12 April 1972|page=1}} '''11-26 April''' South Korean soldiers won their bloodiest battle of the war at An Khe Pass, dislodging PAVN forces to reopen a key supply route. Officially, 75 ROK were killed and another 222 wounded, but this number was disputed by veterans and CNN, with the latter alleging that actual casualties were double the official figures.{{Cite journal |last=Shim |first=Hosub |date=2020 |title=The Battle of An Khe Pass (1972): The Implications of the South Korean Army's Pyrrhic Victory in the Vietnamization Phase of the Vietnam War |journal=International Journal of Military History and Historiography |volume=74 |issue=109 |pages=75–77}} ;12 April A PAVN rocket attack on Da Nang Air Base killed 14 civilians and destroyed a USAF [[Douglas C-47 Skytrain|EC-47]].{{cite web|url=https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/reports/images.php?img=/images/1683/168300010829.pdf|title=United States Military Assistance Command, Vietnam 1972-1973 Command History Volume 1|publisher=United States Military Assistance Command, Vietnam|date=15 July 1973|access-date=14 July 2020|page=44|archive-date=14 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200714094842/https://www.vietnam.ttu.edu/reports/images.php?img=/images/1683/168300010829.pdf|url-status=live}}{{PD-notice}} Approximately 50 men from Company C, 2nd Battalion [[1st Infantry Regiment (United States)|1st Infantry Regiment]] which had been flown into [[Phu Bai Combat Base]] from Danang to provide base security the previous day, refused to go on a combat patrol in the hills west of Phu Bai, but eventually undertook the patrol.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=50 G.I.'s in Vietnam refuse patrol duty, then agree to go|date=13 April 1972|page=1}} The 2nd Battalion commander [[Lieutenant colonel (United States)|Lieutenant colonel]] Frederick P. Mitchell blamed television newsmen and journalists for inciting the combat refusal.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Colonel assails newsmen|date=13 April 1972|page=16}} ;13 April The United States Senate voted 68–16 to approve the [[War Powers Resolution|War Powers Act]], which would limit the power of the President to commit American forces to hostilities without Congressional approval. The legislation then moved on to the House.{{cite news|title=War Powers Limits Voted in Senate|newspaper=Oakland Tribune|date=13 April 1972|page=1}} After two B-52 strikes around Firebase Bastogne/Phu Xuan, the ARVN relief force reported finding 210 PAVN dead.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Enemy captures a half of An Loc; 40 tanks in push|date=14 April 1972|page=1}} In fighting in Kampong Trach the ARVN reported killing 127 PAVN for the loss of 13 ARVN.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Cambodia clash reported|date=14 April 1972|page=14}} ; 13 April – 20 July After several days of artillery strikes, the PAVN [[9th Division (Vietnam)|9th Division]] attacked An Lộc supported by 40 tanks. They captured the northern half of the city but the ARVN defenders held the rest supported by heavy U.S. air attacks. Averell Harriman]] and [[Cyrus Vance]], the two original U.S. negotiators at the Paris Peace Talks, said in a press conference that President Nixon had missed an opportunity in 1969 to end the Vietnam War, at a time when the North Vietnamese had withdrawn most of its combat troops from South Vietnam's northernmost provinces.{{cite news|title=Nixon Ignored Peace Bid, Paris Team Says|newspaper=Oakland Tribune|date=13 August 1972|page=1}} [[Lockheed C-130 Hercules|C-130E Hercules]] #62-1853 of the [[776th Expeditionary Airlift Squadron|776th Tactical Airlift Squadron]] was shot down on takeoff from [[Sóc Trăng Airfield]], killing 30 of 44 passengers and crew on board.{{cite web|url=http://aviation-safety.net/database/record.php?id=19720812-1|title=Lockheed C-130 E Hercules Soc Trang|publisher=Aviation Safety Network|access-date=24 November 2014}} ''The New York Times'' reported on accusations of widespread torture of civilians who had been imprisoned in South Vietnamese jails since the start of the Easter Offensive.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon torture in jails reported|author=Sydney Schanberg|date=13 August 1972|page=1}} ;13 August Former [[U.S. Attorney General]] [[Ramsey Clark]] returned from North Vietnam, where he had traveled as a private individual as part of a factfinding group. news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=861&dat=19720822&id=JY1HAAAAIBAJ&pg=5568,3185027|title=U.S. confirms enemy captured secret missiles|publisher=Washington Post News Service|date=22 The Pentagon announced that a U.S. bomb had inadvertently struck the French mission in Hanoi on 11 October.{{rp|421}} Operation Enhance Plus began with the objective of providing additional military equipment and support to South Vietnam. The media was given its first access to [[Nakhon Phanom Royal Thai Navy Base]] and was informed that U.S. sensors and surveillance along the Ho Chi Minh Trail showed that PAVN infiltration had dropped to negligible levels.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Sensors attune U.S. base in Thailand to movements on Ho Chi Minh Trail|author=Malcolm Browne|date=23 October 1972|page=2}} ;23 October In fighting near Firebases 40 and 41, [[Đức Cơ Camp]] and My Thach near Pleiku, 95 PAVN and one ARVN were reported killed.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Ground fighting widens in South|date=24 October 1972|page=1}} In fighting {{convert|3|mi}} east of [[Phù Mỹ district]] 73 PAVN were killed and 12 captured for the loss of five ARVN. ''The New York Times'' reported that the mood in Cambodia was one of resignation in the face of irresistible forces. A ceasefire would leave the PAVN in control of more than half the country with the PAVN/VC occupying all of eastern Cambodia as a massive base area.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Cambodia: A fear of forces beyond control|author=Craig Whitney|date=23 October 1972|page=1}} Souvanna Phouma said that he expected an Indochina-wide ceasefire to be announced by the end of the month and that in Laos this would take a similar form to the 1961 and 1962 neutralization agreements.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Laotian expecting truce|date=24 October 1972|page=3}} ;24 October Nixon suspended bombing of North Vietnam above the [[20th parallel north|20th parallel]] as a sign of goodwill towards North Vietnam and pressure on Thiệu.{{rp|422}} U.S. advisors were reported to be conducted an intensive retraining program for the entire ARVN with an emphasis on basic infantry tactics and small arms employment due to poor performance during the Easter Offensive, an influx of new replacements and ongoing deficiencies in ARVN training.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. pushing retraining of Saigon's entire army|author=Joseph Treaster|date=25 October 1972|page=1}} Thiệu said that all peace proposals negotiated in Paris were unacceptable and that there were great difficulties in achieving a ceasefire, but that a ceasefire could come quickly. He also said that "The Communists could only hope to win if our ally betrays us and sells us out, but our main ally will never betray us. He has invested so much blood and money."{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Thieu assails peace plan terms, asks guarantee|author=Craig Whitney|date=25 October 1972|page=1}} The USAF dismissed all charges against Lavelle.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Charges against Lavelle dismissed by Air Force|date=25 October 1972|page=16}} ;25 October PAVN/VC conducted 113 attacks across South Vietnam in what was seen as an attempt to seize as much territory as possible before an imminent ceasefire. A rocket attack on Danang Air Base killed one U.S. civilian and nine South Vietnamese civilians outside the base. A rocket attack on Hội An killed four civilians and wounded 35. A rocket attack on Tri Tam {{convert|36|mi}} northwest of Saigon killed ten civilians and one ARVN and wounded 37 civilians.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Enemy presses 113 attacks in apparent drive to gain territory before truce|author=Joseph Treaster|date=26 October 1972|page=14}} North Vietnam broadcast publicly the terms of the draft peace agreement and accused the United States of negotiating in bad faith saying that the terms of a ceasefire agreement had been agreed, but that the U.S. had backed off signing "claiming that it had difficulties in Saigon." South Vietnam's Foreign Minister [[Trần Văn Lắm]] briefed the ambassadors from Australia, Japan, Laos, the Philippines, Thailand and West Germany on the current peace proposals.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Thieu a question|author=Craig Whitney|date=26 October 1972|page=1}} ;26 October Despite South Vietnamese opposition to the draft peace agreement and the charges by North Vietnam that the U.S. was negotiating in bad faith, Kissinger declared "Peace is at hand" in Vietnam and that a final agreement could be achieved after one more three-four day negotiating session. South Vietnam announced that it was "ready to accept a cease-fire" but "would never accept a political settlement which goes against the interests and aspirations of the 17 million South Vietnamese people."{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Doubt is voiced|author=Craig Whitney|date=27 October 1972|page=1}} Xuân Thủy said that the U.S. and North Vietnam had resolved all outstanding points on 17 October, that a ceasefire agreement was scheduled to be signed on 31 October and called on the U.S. to honor that commitment.{{rp|422}} Heavy fighting was reported in Laos, particularly in the Plain of Jars area and near Saravane as each side sought to maximize their territory before any ceasefire.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Laotian troops drive to retake a key southern town before a ceasefire|author=Malcolm Browne|date=27 October 1972|page=20}} ;27 October PAVN/VC conducted 125 attacks across South Vietnam, while ARVN forces were ordered to contest all PAVN/VC attempts to control the countryside before any ceasefire.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon out to win firm grip on villages|date=28 October 1972|page=11}} Speaking at a rally of South Vietnamese political leaders, Thiệu said that his "minimum demand" for a ceasefire was the withdrawal of all North Vietnamese forces from South Vietnam.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Thieu insists that a cease-fire hinges on Hanoi troop pullout|date=28 October 1972|page=1}} ;28 October PAVN/VC conducted 138 attacks across South Vietnam, including seizing 13 hamlets and cutting three highways near Saigon. U.S. aircraft conducted 329 airstrikes over South Vietnam to counter the attacks, including 51 in the Mekong Delta to forestall any attacks there. Allied intelligence said that the PAVN/VC may have been relying on outdated instructions to seize territory before a ceasefire was signed on 31 October, causing them to "jump the gun" and exposing them to strong counter-attacks.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Foe occupies 13 hamlets, cuts 3 roads near Saigon|author=Fox Butterfield|date=29 October 1972|page=1}} Trần Văn Lắm said that the draft peace agreement would amount to a surrender of South Vietnam and was unacceptable. He said that all North Vietnamese forces must be withdrawn and the DMZ reestablished, neither of which were addressed in the agreement.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Aide to Thieu assails plan for truce as 'Surrender'|author=Joseph Treaster|date=29 October 1972|page=1}} ;28 October - 22 February 1973 [[Campaign 972]] was a PAVN offensive that effectively succeeded in cutting Laos in two. The operation ended with the ceasefire pursuant to the [[Vientiane Treaty]] ending the [[Laotian Civil War]].{{rp|394–5}} ;29 October PAVN/VC conducted another 138 attacks across South Vietnam, including seizing 17 hamlets within a {{convert|45|mi}} radius of Saigon and cut Highway 1 west and east of Saigon with 14 PAVN/VC killed. The PAVN fired artillery and conducted ground assaults against three outposts northwest of Kontum and fired artillery into Kontum killing four civilians and wounding 11. In fighting southwest of Quảng Trị, ARVN Airborne killed 49 PAVN for the loss of two killed.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Enemy steps up infiltration near Saigon|author=Fox Butterfield|date=30 October 1972|page=1}} Following a 1,000+ round artillery barrage, the PAVN attacked [[Dak Seang Camp]] forcing its 300 Ranger defenders to abandon it by nightfall.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Communists seize camp in Highlands|author=Craig Whitney|date=31 October 1972|page=1}} South Vietnamese police were reported to have increased patrols and arrests in Saigon and other cities in preparation for the possible ceasefire.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon increasing vigilance in cities|author=Craig Whitney|date=30 October 1972|page=3}} The Nixon Administration said that the peace agreement would not be signed by 31 October, but remained optimistic that the final details would be resolved soon.{{rp|423}} ;30 October The JGS reported that of the 21 hamlets near Saigon occupied by the PAVN/VC, all but six had been recaptured. Four PAVN rockets hit Huế killing two civilians and wounding two. Five PAVN rockets hit a FANK ammunition dump {{convert|8|mi}} southwest of Phnom Penh killing five FANK and wounding 30 others.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Attacks reported in Cambodia|date=31 October 1972|page=4}} ;31 October PAVN forces overran a 300-man Ranger camp {{convert|1|mi}} west of Ba Tơ. In fighting north and south of [[Đăk Tô]], the ARVN reported killing 60 PAVN.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Foe overruns second camp in Highlands|date=1 November 1972|page=1}} PAVN forces again captured Quế Sơn town in the continued seesaw fighting for the area. An ammunition explosion near the [[Thủ Đức Military Academy]] killed three ARVN.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Queson reported lost|date=1 November 1972|page=12}} In one of the final American special forces operations of the war, an intelligence-gathering mission near Cửa Việt Base, Navy SEAL petty officer [[Michael E. Thornton]] saved the life of his commanding officer, Lieutenant [[Thomas R. Norris]]; he would later be awarded the [[Medal of Honor]], the latest action in the war for which it was awarded. There were only a dozen Navy SEALs still in Vietnam at the time of the mission. PAVN/VC conducted more than 117 attacks across South Vietnam, including an attack on an RF/PF outpost {{convert|4|mi}} west of Pleiku that killed eight ARVN. B-52s conducted heavy raids against PAVN infiltration routes in the Central Highlands. U.S. intelligence reported that PAVN reinforcements, including an armored regiment, were moving across the DMZ into Quảng Trị province. ''The New York Times'' reported that the VC cadre numbering 40-60,000 remained intact in South Vietnam and would pose an ongoing threat to the South Vietnamese government control after any ceasefire.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Core of Vietcong surviving war|author=Fox Butterfield|date=5 November 1972|page=1}} On the campaign trail Nixon said that there were "some details still to be negotiated" but he was confident that such a peace agreement would be achieved based on "honor" and not "surrender."{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Nixon hopeful on Vietnam but concedes pact is open|date=5 November 1972|page=1}} McGovern warned Americans not to "buy this Nixon line on peace." saying "He has no plan for ending this war. agreement.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Rogers expects Hanoi will enter final talks soon|author=Bernard Gwertzman|date=6 November 1972|page=1}} ;6 November Three U.S. Army
