Sterba|date=25 November 1972|page=1}} 42 B-52 strikes hit Vinh and Đồng Hới. The JGS reported that 38 PAVN/VC had been killed in fighting near Gò Dầu district.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. keeps up its bombing of North to slow supplies|date=25 November 1972|page=8}} ''The New York Times'' reported that the progress of peace negotiations had thrown Thiệu "off balance".{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Peace activity seen as throwing Thieu off balance|author=Craig R. Whitney|date=25 November 1972|page=5}} ;25 November In two attacks near the ARVN base at Thanh Giao, 74 PAVN and 9 ARVN were reported killed. In fighting north of Quảng Trị, the Marines received 770 rounds of artillery and mortar fire, losing six killed while killing five PAVN.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Heavy B-52 raids on North reduced|date=26 November 1972|page=17}} The peace negotiations ended in an impasse with the parties agreeing to resume discussions on 4 December.{{rp|426}} Anticipating that the peace agreement would require release of all political prisoners, the government of South Vietnam began charging people detained for political reasons with petty crimes, thus ensuring their continued incarceration. [[Amnesty International]] estimated that South Vietnam had imprisoned 200,000 people for political reasons, and would release only 5,000 after the peace agreement came into effect.{{rp|48}} A Gallup poll found that 59% of Americans approved Nixon's handling of the war with 33% opposed.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Gallup Poll backs President's method of ending the war|date=26 November 1972|page=21}} ;26 November In fighting in the foothills southwest of Quảng Trị, Airborne forces killed 32 PAVN for the loss of 16 killed. Two PAVN 122mm rockets hit Quảng Ngãi killing two children and wounding ten other civilians. A PAVN mortar attack on Kontum killed one civilian and wounded six. A PAVN mortar attack on an ARVN base northwest of Saigon killed two ARVN.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Shelling hits Saigon troops in Quangtri|date=27 November 1972|page=10}} ;27 November Heavy fighting continued in the foothills southwest of Quảng Trị, with Airborne forces, supported by 18 B-52 strikes, killing 31 PAVN for the loss of one killed.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Heavy fighting reported in foothills near Quangtri|date=28 November 1972|page=3}} South Vietnamese Marines closed in on Cửa Việt Base supported by B-52 strikes. The Marines received more than 600 rounds of mortar fire and killed 12 PAVN for the loss of five Marines.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. planes, in bombing error, kill 19 civilians near Danang|date=29 November 1972|page=1}} ''The New York Times'' reported that more than 10,000 U.S. civilian advisers and technicians would remain in South Vietnam to support South Vietnamese forces after any ceasefire.{{rp|426}} China and North Vietnam signed an agreement in Peking providing for Chinese aid in 1973.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Peking signs pact to aid Hanoi in '73|author=Tilman Durdin|date=28 November 1972|page=4}} ;28 November Six U.S. fighter-bombers accidentally bombed civilians {{convert|2.5|mi}} southwest of [[Hội An (city)|Hội An]] killing 21 and wounding 30. A VC rocket attack on Đức Phổ killed four civilians and wounded eight. ;29 November Bad weather reduced U.S. airstrikes across Vietnam and slowed down South Vietnamese offensive operations in Quảng Trị province.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon reports drive is slowed|date=30 November 1972|page=17}} ''The New York Times'' reported on the massive influx of refugees into Phnom Penh from the countryside, the huge disparity of wealth within the city and corruption with the government.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Cambodian war enriches the corrupt, debases the poor|author=Sydney Schanberg|date=30 November 1972|page=16}} ;30 November Nixon met with the Joint Chiefs of Staff who approved the outline of the peace plan. It was reported that Nixon had advised that flagrant violations of the ceasefire would be met with airstrikes. Nixon subsequently met with Nguyễn Phú Duc, Thiệu's special envoy. The White House stated that it would no longer provide public announcements on U.S. troop withdrawals now that the number had fallen below 27,000.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=President meets with Joint Chiefs on truce accord|author=Bernard Gwertzman|date=1 December 1972|page=1}} ==December== ;1 December The U.S. reported no military deaths in Indochina in the preceding week for the first time since January 1965. South Vietnamese losses were 480 killed while PAVN/VC losses were estimated at 1,896 killed. Thirty PAVN rockets hit Bien Hoa Air Base.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=No U.S. deaths reported in last week in Indochina|date=1 December 1972|page=3}} PAVN rockets fired on Kompong Cham killed two civilians and wounded 20.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Cambodian city shelled|date=1 December 1972|page=3}} ARVN Major general [[Trần Thanh Phong]], deputy commander of Military Region II, was killed when the RVNAF plane he was travelling on crashed in bad weather on approach to [[Tuy Hoa Air Base]]. Four other South Vietnamese and two [[USAID]] officials were also killed in the crash.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=South Vietnamese General and six others, including two Americans, die in plane crash|date=2 December 1972|page=7}} In scattered fighting across South Vietnam 85 PAVN/VC and two ARVN were reported killed. ''The New York Times'' reported that VC radio was increasingly broadcasting the names of members of the [[Provisional Revolutionary Government of the Republic of South Vietnam]] in an apparent attempt to popularize them after the ceasefire.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Vietcong try to popularize possible postwar figures|author=Craig R. Whitney|date=1 December 1972|page=3}} ;2 December South Vietnamese Marines were reported to be bogged down in heavy rain in Quảng Trị, despite B-52 strikes on PAVN positions.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon drive near DMZ reported bogged down|date=3 December 1972|page=2}} ''The New York Times'' reported that in Saigon the expectation was that a peace agreement, substantially similar to the October proposal, would be finalized within the next few days.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon expects Cease-Fire pact in week with a formal signature About Dec. 15|author=Craig R. Whitney|date=3 December 1972|page=1}} ;3 December The Rangers abandoned a position {{convert|8|mi}} southwest of Kontum, killing five PAVN, while an attack on Mo Duc was repulsed with nine PAVN killed. A U.S. AH-1 was shot down by an SA-7 {{convert|50|mi}} northwest of Saigon, both crewmen were rescued.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Foe again shells BienHoa Air Base|date=4 December 1972|page=16}} U.S. aircraft were reported to have conducted more than 90 airstrikes against supply lines in North Vietnam.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. reports heavy raids to cut enemy's supplies|date=5 December 1972|page=3}} ;4 December Kissinger returned to Paris for further meetings with Lê Đức Thọ. Kissinger claimed that the North Vietnamese had changed their position on 20 points agreed to previously.{{rp|427}} Ten PAVN rockets hit Bien Hoa Air Base causing no damage. In fighting in Quảng Trị, northeast of the city the Marines killed 37 PAVN and captured one for the loss of one Marine killed, while south of the city Airborne forces killed 24 PAVN. ARVN forces repulsed a PAVN attack on Ngo Trang {{convert|7|mi}} north of Kontum killing 65 PAVN for the loss of four killed.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon's airport is hit by rockets|date=6 December 1972|page=19}} RLA forces were reported to have killed 30 PAVN in Saravane.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Battle for Saravane continues|date=5 December 1972|page=3}} ;5 December The Paris talks were suspended for a day amid reports that Kissinger was seeking to clarify the status of PAVN troops remaining in South Vietnam after a ceasefire.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Hanoi troop plan said to be issue at peace parley|author=William Beecher|date=6 December 1972|page=1}} New Australian Prime Minister [[Gough Whitlam]] announced an end to [[Conscription in Australia|conscription]] and that Australia would pursue diplomatic ties with China.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=New Australian leader end draft|author=Robert Trumbull|date=6 December 1972|page=1}} PAVN forces attacked an outpost {{convert|9|mi}} north of Kontum with 35 ARVN reported missing and 15 PAVN killed. Marines near Quảng Trị killed 21 PAVN for the loss of three killed. ARVN forces killed 33 PAVN for the loss of six killed in southwest Pleiku province.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. planes strike near Saigon base in reprisal raid|author=Sylvan Fox|date=7 December 1972|page=1}} B-52s attacked PAVN supply depots near Dong Hoi and PAVN positions near Quảng Trị and Kontum. RLA forces captured Paksong on the Bolaven Plateau.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Laotian gain reported|date=6 December 1972|page=19}} ;6 December Peace talks resumed again in Paris after Kissinger received instructions from Washington.{{rp|427}} A PAVN rocket attack on Tan Son Nhut Air Base killed eight South Vietnamese and one American and five civilians in a nearby village and damaged two U.S. rescue helicopters. PAVN forces also attacked [[Thủ Đức, Ho Chi Minh City|Thủ Đức]], {{convert|10|mi}} north of Saigon. U.S. aircraft conducted airstrikes against suspected launch sites around the base. Nine B-52 strikes and more than 90 tactical airstrikes were conducted against PAVN supply lines in North Vietnam. ;7 December The Paris peace talks continued with the most contentious issue reported to be the status of PAVN troop after the ceasefire, with the South Vietnamese government insisting that all PAVN troops must be withdrawn. The State Department was said to have alerted more than 100 staff for deployment to South Vietnam to monitor the ceasefire.{{rp|427}} Airborne forces overran a PAVN fortified position {{convert|6|mi}} southwest of Quảng Trị killing 20 PAVN for the loss of three Airborne soldiers. The bodies of a further 30 PAVN killed in airstrikes were also found. ARVN forces captured the site used for launching the rocket attacks on Tan Son Nhut finding the bodies of 30 PAVN/VC killed by airstrikes.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=B-52s bomb DMZ area|date=8 December 1972|page=10}} 35 B-52 strikes and 90 tactical airstrikes were made against PAVN positions and supply lines north of the DMZ with more than 600 tons of bombs dropped. Four PAVN frogmen blew up the Hong Kong freighter ''Bright Star'' docked in Phnom Penh killing one crewman and three Cambodian laborers, sentries killed three of the frogmen while the fourth escaped.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Ship blown up at Phnonpenh|date=8 December 1972|page=10}} ;8 December 27 B-52 and 40 tactical airstrikes were mounted against North Vietnam. The South Vietnamese government reported 82 attacks across the country resulting in 244 PAVN/VC killed for the loss of 16 ARVN.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. keeps up its bombing of DMZ area|date=9 December 1972|page=4}} Pathet Lao forces started a new offensive against RLA positions on the Plain of Jars overrunning two RLA positions.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Enemy hits hard at Laos positions|author=Malcolm Browne|date=12 December 1972|page=9}} ;9 December Airstrikes around the DMZ continued for a third day with more than 20 B-52 and 60 tactical airstrikes. Airborne forces killed 30 PAVN and captured two for the loss of seven killed in fighting in the foothills west of Quảng Trị.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Demilitarized Zone of Vietnam under heavy bombing 3d day|date=10 December 1972|page=6}} ;10 December The South Vietnamese government reported a decline in PAVN/VC attacks across the country. At Quảng Trị, Airborne forces killed 53 PAVN. In fighting near Tam Kỳ ARVN forces killed 40 PAVN/VC. In the Mekong Delta the VC attacked two RF/PF outposts killing 16 RF/PF and their dependents. 18 B-52 strikes were mounted against North Vietnam as far north as Đồng Hới, while 24 strikes were made in South Vietnam.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Enemy attacks decline in South|date=11 December 1972|page=23}} Presidential military aide General [[Alexander Haig]] briefed Nixon on the progress of the peace talks.{{rp|427}} ;11 December B-52s continued strikes on North Vietnam as far north as Đồng Hới and with other raids north of Saigon. Following the tip of a defector, the ARVN intercepted a PAVN battalion infiltrating from Cambodia and killed 79 PAVN in a jungle area {{convert|42|mi}} northwest of Saigon.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Bombing is heavy over Saigon area|date=12 December 1972|page=8}} ;12 December Thiệu proposed an indefinite ceasefire to begin before Christmas and the exchange of prisoners between South and North Vietnam, however he said that he still opposed the "false peace" in the draft peace agreement.{{rp|2}}{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Thieu proposes a holiday truce; POW exchange|author=Sylvan Fox|date=12 December 1972|page=1}} The PAVN battalion which had infiltrated from Cambodia retreated into the Parrot's Beak area. ARVN forces killed 30 PAVN/VC {{convert|6|mi}} west of Cà Mau. Four ARVN were killed in fighting near Bearcat Base. B-52s continued strikes north of the DMZ for a sixth day.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon reports Hanoi unit flees|date=13 December 1972|page=11}} The Pathet Lao proposed an immediate ceasefire to be supervised by the Pathet Lao, Royal Lao Government and the International Control Commission, with the withdrawal of all U.S. forces within 90 days of signing and the formation of a coalition government.{{rp|427}} ;13 December The peace talks ended with the outstanding issue being Thiệu's insistence on South Vietnamese control over all its territory, which would require that all North Vietnamese forces be withdrawn.{{rp|428}} U.S. sources reported that more than 100 PAVN tanks and thousands of soldiers had started moving from North Vietnam through mountain passes onto the Ho Chi Minh Trail in Laos. While B-52s struck the passes, tactical airstrikes were limited by bad weather, however more than 190 strikes were conducted in northern South Vietnam.{{rp|428}} RLA forces captured Muong Phalane from PAVN forces after a monthlong operation.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Laotian troops capture an important town near the Ho Chi Minh Trail after month-long campaign|author=Malcolm Browne|date=14 December 1972|page=13}} ;14 December Nixon met Kissinger and Haig in Washington and the three of them agreed on an intensified bombing campaign against North Vietnam to, in the words of Haig, "strike hard... and keep on striking until the enemy's will was broken." The weapon of choice would be the B-52, which had never been used before to strike targets in the vicinity of Hanoi and the city of Haiphong.{{rp|143–4}} Nixon ordered the Joint Chiefs of Staff to commence planning for the operation.{{rp|428}} 14 B-52 missions, by up to three planes each, were conducted against North Vietnam dropping 1,260 tons of bombs on supply bases around Đồng Hới with a further 19 missions conducted in South Vietnam.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=B-52s fly 33 missions|date=15 December 1972|page=17}} A PAVN rocket attack on Bien Hoa Air Base killed six civilians in nearby houses. PAVN/VC mortar attacks caused a fire at a fuel depot on the Saigon river and a PAVN/VC sapper attack caused massive explosion at an ammunition dump {{convert|7|mi}} southeast of Saigon.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Base at Bien Hoa is shelled by foe|date=15 December 1972|page=17}} All members of the [[New Zealand in the Vietnam War#New Zealand Army Training Team Vietnam (1 NZATTV & 2 NZATTV)|New Zealand Army Training Team Vietnam]] were withdrawn from South Vietnam ending New Zealand's involvement in the war.{{cite book|last=Jessup|first=John|title=An encyclopedic dictionary of conflict and conflict resolution, 1945-1996|edition=1998|year=1998|publisher=[[Greenwood Publishing Group]]|isbn= 0-313-28112-2|page=523}} ;15 December 48 B-52s dropped over 1,200 tons of bombs on targets near Đồng Hới with a further seven missions around Quảng Trị and three {{convert|18|mi}} southwest of An Lộc. In fighting {{convert|2|mi}} southeast of Quảng Trị Airborne units killed 44 PAVN for the loss of one killed. Five PAVN and two ARVN were killed in fighting near Đức Cơ Camp. Eighteen PAVN were killed in fighting near Thanh Giao camp near Pleiku. Three rockets attacks were made against Bien Hoa Air Base killing two civilians.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Heaviest B-52 raids strike at supplies in North|author=Sylvan Fox|date=16 December 1972|page=14}} A Federal court heard testimony that for eight years heroin had been smuggled into the U.S. concealed in the bodies of U.S. war dead.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Drug feared sent in bodies of G.I.s|author=Sylvan Fox|date=17 December 1972|page=21}} ;16 December At a press conference, Kissinger said that the negotiations had failed to achieve what Nixon regarded as a "just and fair agreement" to end the war and that "the United States will not be blackmailed...stampeded...[or] charmed into an agreement until its conditions are right." Kissinger also warned South Vietnam that "no other party will have a veto over our actions." but blamed North Vietnam for failing to reach an agreement.{{rp|145}} North Vietnam charged that Kissinger had once again breached the agreement not to discuss the content of the talks, denied that they had introduced new conditions and blamed the U.S. for the impasse.{{rp|428}} The impasse centred around the recognition of South Vietnamese sovereignty (including the withdrawal of PAVN forces) and the composition of the supervisory body.{{rp|428}} Thai premier [[Thanom Kittikachorn]] approved the use of Nakhon Phanom Royal Thai Navy Base for the relocation of MACV and 7th Air Force headquarters following the implementation of any ceasefire in Vietnam.{{rp|428}} The PAVN fired 20 rockets at Bien Hoa Air Base killing two civilians while ARVN 18th Division commander, Brigadier general [[Lê Minh Đảo]] said that PAVN forces were building up near the base. B-52 flew eight missions against North Vietnam and 22 missions in South Vietnam including five near the DMZ.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon reporting an enemy build-Up near Bienhoa base|date=17 December 1972|page=33}} ;17 December American warplanes dropped new naval mines off the coast of North Vietnam, including at Haiphong and other locations above the 20th parallel.{{rp|145}} Airborne forces killed 151 PAVN in a two day battle around Firebase Anne, {{convert|8|mi}} southwest of Quảng Trị for the loss of two Airborne killed. In the Central Highlands 50 PAVN and five ARVN were reported killed, while 36 B-52s dropped 1,000 tons of bombs on PAVN staging areas {{convert|30|mi}} southwest of Pleiku. Five B-52 missions were flown against North Vietnam just north of the western DMZ.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon reports heavy fighting, killing 151 near Quang Tri City|date=18 December 1972|page=4}} ;18 December [[Operation Linebacker II]] began. Better known as the "Christmas bombings", 129 B-52s and smaller tactical aircraft struck at targets in North Vietnam, including around the city of Hanoi. North Vietnam shot down three B-52s.{{rp|145–6}} The White House stated that the raids would continue "until such time as a settlement is arrive at" including the release of all U.S. POWs and an internationally recognized ceasefire was in force, adding that "we are not going to allow the peace talks to be used as cover for another offensive."{{rp|429}} B-52D [[Tail gunner]] Staff Sgt Samuel Turner shot down a VPAF MiG-21, scoring the first of only two air gunner kills of the war.{{rp|429}} 60 B-52s hit target around Quảng Trị in support of ARVN Airborne units fighting at Firebase Anne.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Third day of heavy fighting is reported around Quang Tri City|date=19 December 1972|page=14}} The last Australian soldiers of the [[Australian Army Training Team Vietnam]] left South Vietnam, ending Australia's involvement in the war.{{rp|430}} A rocket attack on [[Luang Prabang Airport]] damaged two aircraft and a fuel depot.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Airport attacked|date=18 December 1972|page=4}} The House Armed Services Committee held that the raids on North Vietnam approved by USAF General John D. Lavelle, "were not only proper, but essential."{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Lavelle's raids are held proper|date=19 December 1972|page=13}} ;19 December Hanoi described the renewed bombing as barbaric and insane.{{rp|430}} Xuân Thủy responded to Kissinger's remarks of 16 December, accusing the U.S. of derailing the peace talks by attempting to introduce 126 changes to the draft October peace agreement at the meeting on 20 November.{{rp|146}} Three B-52s and two fighter-bombers were reported to have been lost with 15 crewmen missing in the Linebacker attacks.{{rp|430}} Haig met with Thiệu in Saigon to deliver a letter from Nixon. Nixon said it was his "irrevocable intention" to achieve a peace agreement with North Vietnam, preferably with the cooperation of South Vietnam, "but, if necessary, alone." He pledged continue military support to South Vietnam if Hanoi violated the agreement. Haig told Thiệu, "Under no circumstances will President Nixon accept a veto from Saigon in regard to a peace agreement."{{rp|148}} North Vietnamese coastal artillery fire hit the {{USS|Goldsborough|DDG-20|6}} killing three crewmen.{{rp|430}} The Royal Lao Government responded to the Pathet Lao 12 December peace proposal rejecting its terms.{{rp|427}} ;20 December Radio Hanoi reported that 215 people had been killed and 325 wounded in Hanoi and 45 killed and 131 wounded in Haiphong in the raids, while the U.S. denied accusations they were involved in terror bombing and said only military targets were being struck.{{rp|430}} North Vietnam shot down six B-52s, but depleted their supply of SAMs.{{rp|147}} Thiệu kept Haig waiting for five hours before seeing him. He attempted to persuade Haig that the U.S. should require the withdrawal of all PAVN soldiers from South Vietnam in any peace agreement. Haig suggested to Nixon that if a peace agreement was not reached the U.S. could consider a unilateral disengagement from South Vietnam in exchange for the return of American POWs by North Vietnam.{{rp|148–9}} In fighting around Quảng Trị, Airborne and Marine forces killed 154 PAVN for the loss of eight killed. Despite clear weather only 50 airstrikes were conducted in I Corps as U.S. air assets concentrated against North Vietnam.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Saigon reports two battles|date=21 December 1972|page=13}} FANK reported that fighting had broken out {{convert|12|mi}} south of Phnom Penh and around the besieged town of Kompong Thom with more than 30 FANK soldiers killed in the preceding two weeks.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Fighting near Phnom Penh|date=21 December 1972|page=13}} ; 21 December Fearing additional losses, the U.S. deployed only 30 B-52s to bomb mostly around Hanoi and Haiphong, nevertheless, four more B-52s were shot down. B-52 crew members complained that the flight patterns assigned to them increased their risk. Flight patterns were changed for subsequent days.{{rp|149–50}} The Cuban and Egyptian embassies in Hanoi were hit by bombs or debris, as were Soviet and Chinese ships in Haiphong.{{rp|430}} The North Vietnamese and Vietcong delegations walked out of the Paris peace talks in protest at the renewed bombing, but called for another session on 28 December.{{rp|430}} Leonid Brezhnev, speaking at an event marking the 50th anniversary of the Soviet Union, condemned the U.S. bombing and said that U.S.-Soviet relations hinged on the ending of the war.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Brezhnev links relations with U.S. to War's end|author=Hedrick Smith|date=21 December 1972|page=1}} In fighting around Quảng Trị, 83 PAVN and 10 South Vietnamese were reported killed.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Ground action light except in the region around Quang Tri|date=22 December 1972|page=12}} FANK command reported that PAVN forces began an "all-out attack" on Konmpng Thom.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=All-out attack reported|date=22 December 1972|page=12}} FANK and ARVN forces began a joint offensive near Kompong Chrey, {{convert|16|mi}} inside Cambodia.{{rp|431}} A USAF AC-130A gunship operated by the 16th Special Operations Squadron was shot down by anti-aircraft fire near Ban Lao Ngam, killing all 14 crewmen.{{rp|430–1}} ; 22 December The White House said that the bombing would continue until North Vietnam decided to resume negotiations "in a spirit of goodwill and in a constructive attitude."{{rp|431}} Nixon offered to suspend the U.S. bombing north of the 20th parallel on 31 December if Hanoi agreed to a 3 January meeting in Paris.{{rp|149}} [[File:Bach Mai 21 December 1972.jpg|thumb|right|Bach Mai Airfield bomb damage assessment]] Bach Mai Hospital in Hanoi was struck by seven bombs killing 18 people. The U.S. aircraft were targeting the adjacent Bach Mai Airfield, the VPAF's air defense command and control center.{{cite journal|title=Linebacker and the Law of War|journal=Air University Review |volume=37|publisher=United States Air Force|year=1985|page=25}} 41 U.S. religious leaders signed a letter condemning the bombing and there were antiwar protests in [[Times Square]], New York.{{rp|431}} ; 23 December USAF officials claimed that the performance of B-52s over Hanoi proved that the aircraft could penetrate Soviet air defenses, but declined to comment on North Vietnamese air defense performance for the first time. The East German embassy was damaged by bombs/debris.{{rp|431}} Opposition to the bombing was extensive among American politicians. In the Senate, 45 Senators responding to a poll opposed the bombing as compared to 19 who supported it.{{rp|153}} PAVN forces supported by PT-76 tanks attacked an RLA held bridge over the Se Bang River {{convert|24|mi}} north of [[Seno, Laos]], capturing the position but losing 3 PT-76s destroyed. Continued fighting also occurred at Saravane which had been subject to intensive PAVN artillery bombardment.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=A Hanoi battalion in Laos said to seize key bridge|author=Malcolm Browne |date=24 December 1972|page=3}} ''Reuters'' reported on the plight of [[Amerasian]] children in South Vietnam who were shunned by society and often given up to orphanages.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Children of G.I.'s shunned in Vietnam|date=24 December 1972|page=3}} ;24 December South Vietnam began a Christmas ceasefire from 18:00 24 December to 18:00 25 December. The U.S. observed a similar 24-hour ceasefire in South Vietnam, while halting its raids on North Vietnam for 36 hours.{{rp|431}}{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. renews raids in North Vietnam after lull ends|date=26 December 1972|page=1}} Xuân Thủy said that North Vietnam would not return to negotiations until the U.S. stopped bombing north of the 20th parallel.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Thuy rejects peace talks while U.S. raids continue|author=Bernard Gwertzman|date=25 December 1972|page=1}} [[Bob Hope]] performed his ninth and final Christmas show in South Vietnam at Tan Son Nhut Air Base. He endorsed the renewed bombing of North Vietnam and was awarded South Vietnam's highest civilian medal.{{rp|431}} ;25 December Hanoi claimed that thousands of civilians had been killed and more than 40,000 tons of bombs dropped in the U.S. "carpet-bombing" of Hanoi and Haiphong.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Hanoi reports heavy toll|date=26 December 1972|page=8}} South Vietnam claimed that there had been 58 violations of the ceasefire resulting in 60 PAVN/VC, 40 ARVN and five civilians killed.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Truce violations charged|date=26 December 1972|page=8}} A PAVN rocket attack on Da Nang Air Base killed two civilians and damaged five U.S. helicopters. U.S. aircraft attacked a 50 vehicle PAVN convoy near An Lộc, destroying 11 vehicles.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Da Nang base area is hit by 35 rockets|date=27 December 1972|page=7}} FANK command reported that 17 soldiers had been killed and more than 265 were missing in heavy fighting less than {{convert|2|mi}} from the center of Kompong Thom.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Cambodians under attack|date=26 December 1972|page=8}} ; 26 December After the Christmas truce, the U.S. conducted the largest B-52 raid of the war utilizing 120 B-52s. The U.S. lost two airplanes. 215 civilians were killed by bombs dropped on a heavily populated area of Hanoi. North Vietnam proposed a resumption of peace talks on 8 January.{{rp|150}} ; 27 December MACV issued a detailed report of military targets hit in the Linebacker raids but made no comment on civilian losses.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=U.S. lists targets of heavy attacks in North Vietnam|author=Joseph Treaster|date=28 December 1972|page=1}} In fighting around Quảng Trị, 69 PAVN were killed for the loss of five South Vietnamese. An RVNAF F-5 accidentally bombed a village {{convert|5|mi}} north of Bien Hoa Air Base killing nine civilians.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Allied plane kills 9 in bombing error|date=28 December 1972|page=2}} Thiệu issued decree law 60 which effectively banned all parties other than his Democracy Party, forcing all his political opposition to dissolve or go underground.{{rp|432}} The Cambodian Government acknowledged that more than 100,000 soldiers claimed to be serving in the military, more than one third of the army, did not exist and were ghosts created by corrupt officers.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=One-Third of army in Cambodia found to be nonexistent|author=Sydney Schanberg|date=28 December 1972|page=1}} Australia ceased all military aid to South Vietnam and ended a training program for Cambodian troops in Australia.{{rp|432}} ;28 December In fighting around Quảng Trị, 138 PAVN were killed and 10 captured for the loss of 29 South Vietnamese. A PAVN rocket attack on a training center near Da Nang killed three ARVN.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=South Vietnamese training post near Da Nang is hit by rockets|date=29 December 1972|page=3}} ;29 December ''The New York Times'' reported that B-52 crews on [[Guam]] were shaken by their losses over North Vietnam in what was described as "the greatest air-defense system in history."{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=The war is suddenly grim for the B-52 fliers on Guam|author=Richard Halloran|date=29 December 1972|page=1}} Austria, Belgium, Italy, the Netherlands and Sweden all condemned the Linebacker bombings.{{rp|432}} ;30 December Nixon ordered an end to Operation Linebacker II, but with bombing permitted south of the 20th parallel. Negotiations were scheduled to resume in Paris on January 8. Of 200 B-52s engaged in the operation, 15 were shot down as well as 11 other aircraft, while Hanoi claimed that 34 B-52s had been shot down. 61 B-52 crewmen were killed, captured, or missing. Prior to Linebacker II, during seven years of bombing, only one B-52 had been shot down. Destruction of North Vietnam's military and industrial capacity was substantial. North Vietnam said that 1,623 civilians had been killed in Hanoi and Haiphong, although most civilians had been evacuated from the cities before the bombing.{{rp|150–3}}{{rp|55}} 80 percent of North Vietnam's electrical power production capability had been eliminated. Nixon warned North Vietnam that the bombing would resume if the peace talks collapsed again. Many U.S. officials believed that the operation had been counterproductive given the losses incurred and Congressional and international opposition it has provoked.{{rp|432–3}} North Vietnam denied yeidling to the U.S. attacks, declared victory and claimed that heavy losses of American aircraft was the motive behind the bombing halt. General [[Maxwell Taylor]], former Ambassador to South Vietnam, said terminating America's commitment to South Vietnam even without a peace agreement should be considered by the President.{{rp|153}} U.S. intelligence sources said that North Vietnam had not sent policy directives to its forces in South Vietnam for over two months due to confusion over the status of the Paris peace talks resulting in "uncertainty" among its forces.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Hanoi said to have left its units in South unguided for 2 months|author=Fox Butterfield|date=31 December 1972|page=6}} ; 31 December The South Vietnamese government announced that it would observe a 24-hour New Year ceasefire beginning at 18:00 on 31 December and ending at 18:00 on 1 January 1973.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=Military confirms end of raids in North|author=Joseph Treaster|date=31 December 1972|page=3}} The U.S. refused to confirm if it would observe a ceasefire and conducted 211 airstrikes over South Vietnam and some strikes over North Vietnam before the South Vietnamese ceasefire came into effect.{{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|title=All U.S. bombing believed halted for the holiday|author=Fox Butterfield|date=1 January 1973|page=1}} U.S. military personnel in South Vietnam numbered 24,200.{{rp|433}} ;31 December - 5 February 1973 [[Operation Maharat II]] was an RLA offensive to seize the intersection of Routes 7 and 13 from the Pathet Lao.
